blocks.html: Science starts with noticing. A scientist looks closely, listens, smells and feels (but never tastes anything in a lab), and writes down what she finds. Then she asks a question she could test.
An observation is something you notice with your senses or a tool: "The puddle got smaller by noon." A hypothesis is a guess about why that you can test: "The sun dried the puddle."

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Hand lens
Ruler
Thermometer
Balance
Timer
Notebook

blocks.cap: Tools help your senses: a hand lens sees small things, a ruler measures, a thermometer reads temperature, a balance compares mass and a timer counts seconds. The notebook remembers.

blocks.html: Good questions can be tested. "Why are flowers pretty?" is hard to test. "Do bean seeds sprout faster in a warm room or a cool room?" can be tested with seeds, two rooms and a calendar.

blocks.title: Observation or guess?
blocks.q: Mia writes: "The ice cube on the plate melted in 20 minutes. I think the warm air melted it."
steps: "The ice cube melted in 20 minutes" is what she saw and timed: an observation.
"I think the warm air melted it" is her idea about why: a hypothesis she could test.
blocks.a: The first sentence is an observation; the second is a hypothesis.

blocks.html: Writing a guess as if you saw it. "The dog was hungry" is a guess; "the dog ate all its food in one minute" is what you observed.

items: Sit by a window or in the yard for five minutes with a notebook.
Write five observations: colors, sounds, things that move, the sky.
Pick one and write a question you could test, like "Do more birds come to the yard in the morning or the afternoon?"

blocks.html: Going further. The Handbook of Nature-Study is full of things to observe outdoors, and the Science Lab lets you test ideas on screen.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-5-ETS1 Engineering Design

blocks.html: Sam wants to know if plant food helps bean plants grow. He gives one plant food and leaves one without. But he also puts the fed plant in the sunny window and the other in a dark corner. When the fed plant grows taller, what made the difference?
He cannot tell! He changed two things at once: the food and the light.
In a fair test you change only one thing (the thing you are testing), keep everything else the same, and measure the result. Do it more than once to be sure.

blocks.name: sciexp-bars
blocks.cap: A fair test: same pots, same soil, same water and the same sunny window. Only the plant food was different.

head: Change
Keep the same
Measure
rows: Light, water, soil, pot, kind of seed

blocks.title: Find the problem
blocks.q: Lily tests which ball bounces higher. She drops the red ball from her waist and the blue ball from over her head.
steps: She is testing the ball, so only the ball should change.
But the drop height changed too, and a higher drop makes a higher bounce.
blocks.a: Not fair. Drop both balls from the same height onto the same floor.

blocks.html: Changing two things at once, or testing only one time. One plant can be sick by bad luck; three plants each way gives a fairer answer.

items: Get two paper towels of different brands and two cups of water with the same amount.
Dip the corner of each towel into the water for the same number of seconds.
Measure how high the water climbs on each with a ruler. Which brand soaks up more? What did you keep the same?

blocks.html: Going further. In the Pendulums lab, change only the length, then only the weight, and see which one changes the swing.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-5-ETS1-3: plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled

blocks.html: Scientists all over the world use the same units, the metric system, so they can share results. Its units grow by tens, hundreds and thousands, which makes them easy to change.

blocks.name: sciexp-measure
blocks.cap: Line the end of the object up with the 0 mark, not the end of the ruler. This pencil is 7.5 cm long.

blocks.name: sciexp-measure
blocks.cap: Read a liquid at eye level, at the bottom of its curved top. This cylinder holds 40 mL.

blocks.html: Always write the unit. "The table is 2" could mean 2 meters or 2 centimeters, a big difference!

blocks.title: Change the units
blocks.q: A string is 3 meters long. How many centimeters is that?
steps: 1 meter is 100 centimeters.

blocks.html: Starting at 1 on the ruler, or reading a measuring cup from above. Start at 0, and bend down so your eyes are level with the liquid.

items: Measure your hand span, a book and a spoon in centimeters.
Pour water into a kitchen measuring cup and read it at eye level, then from above. Are they different?
Weigh a bag of flour or rice on a kitchen scale and find its mass on the label. Do they agree?

blocks.html: Going further. The Math Ladder has whole lessons on measuring and changing units.

sources.name: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), "SI Units" (the metric system)

blocks.html: Your chair, a glass of juice and the air you breathe have something in common: they are all matter.
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. All matter is made of tiny pieces called particles, far too small to see.

blocks.name: sciexp-particles
blocks.cap: Particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas. The particles are always moving, even in a solid.

blocks.html: Is air matter? Blow up a balloon: the air pushes the balloon outward, so the air takes up space. A pumped-up ball weighs a little more than the same ball when it is flat, so air has mass too.
We cannot see air because its particles are spread far apart and are clear. We can feel it as wind, and we see it push a sail or fill a balloon.

blocks.title: Matter or not?
blocks.q: Which of these are matter: a rock, milk, the steam over a hot bath, a shadow, a song?
steps: A rock, milk and steam have mass and take up space.
A shadow is only where light is blocked; a song is sound, a kind of energy.
blocks.a: Rock, milk and steam are matter. A shadow and a song are not.

blocks.html: Thinking air is "nothing". Push an upside-down cup straight down into a bowl of water: the air inside keeps most of the water out.

items: Stuff a dry paper towel into the bottom of a clear cup.
Turn the cup upside down and push it straight down into a bowl of water. Hold it there, then lift it straight up.
Is the towel dry? The air in the cup took up space, so the water could not get in.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-PS1-1: matter is made of particles too small to be seen

blocks.html: Ice, water and steam are all the same stuff: water. They are three states of matter.

head: State
Shape
Amount (volume)
Particles
rows: Takes the shape of its container

blocks.name: sciexp-particles
blocks.cap: Solid, liquid and gas.

blocks.html: A solid keeps its shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill the whole space it is in.

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Brick
Milk
Air in a balloon
Ice
Honey
Rock

blocks.cap: Tap a card, then the state it belongs in.

blocks.title: Sand: solid or liquid?
blocks.q: You can pour sand from a bucket. Is sand a liquid?
steps: Look at one grain with a hand lens.
Each grain keeps its own shape, and it does not flow on its own when you tip it a little.
blocks.a: Sand is a solid, made of many tiny solid grains.

blocks.html: Thinking anything that pours is a liquid. Sugar, salt and sand pour because they are many small solid pieces.

items: Pour the same amount of water into a tall glass, a bowl and a plate.
Does the water change shape? Does the amount change? (Pour each back into a measuring cup to check.)

blocks.html: Going further. In Gas in a Box you can watch gas particles bounce around and push on the walls.
Put an ice cube in a warm hand and it melts. Leave water in the freezer and it freezes. Heat a pot of water and it boils away. Matter can change state when it is heated or cooled.
Heating: solid → liquid is melting; liquid → gas is evaporating (or boiling, when it bubbles). Cooling: gas → liquid is condensing; liquid → solid is freezing.

blocks.name: sciexp-measure
blocks.cap: Water freezes and ice melts at 0 °C (32 °F).

blocks.html: Heat makes particles move faster. When they move fast enough, they break out of their tight solid pattern (melting) or escape into the air (evaporating). Cooling slows them down so they stick together again.

blocks.title: What state?
blocks.q: A puddle is at −5 °C on a winter morning. Is it ice or water?
steps: Water freezes at 0 °C.
−5 °C is colder than 0 °C.

blocks.html: Thinking the white "steam" over a kettle is the gas. Water vapor is invisible. The white mist is tiny drops of liquid water made when the vapor cools in the air.
Melting does not change the mass. If 100 grams of ice melt, you have 100 grams of water.

items: Put an ice cube on a plate in the sun and one on a plate in the shade. Which melts first?
Breathe on a cold mirror or window. The fog is water vapor from your breath condensing into tiny drops.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-PS1-2: the total weight of matter is conserved when it changes form

blocks.html: Stir raisins into cereal and you have a mixture: each part keeps its own look and taste, and you can pick the raisins back out.
A mixture is two or more things mixed together that keep their own properties. A solution is a mixture in which one thing dissolves evenly into another, like sugar in tea.

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Cereal and raisins: a mixture
Salt water: a solution
Sand and shells: a mixture
Lemonade: a solution

blocks.cap: Mixtures you can pick apart, and solutions you cannot see the parts of.

blocks.html: You can separate mixtures: pick out pieces by hand, pour through a sieve or filter, pull iron filings out with a magnet, or let the water evaporate to get dissolved salt back.
The salt in salt water is not gone. It broke into pieces too small to see, spread through the water. Taste it, or let the water dry up, and the salt is there.

blocks.title: Mass in a solution
blocks.q: You stir 20 g of salt into 200 g of water. What is the mass of the salt water?
steps: Dissolving does not destroy any matter.

blocks.html: Thinking dissolved salt has disappeared, so the salt water weighs the same as the water alone.

items: Stir a spoonful of salt into a small glass of warm water until you cannot see it.
Pour a little onto a dark plate and leave it in a sunny spot for a day or two.
When the water has evaporated, the salt crystals are left behind.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-PS1-3: identify materials based on their properties

blocks.html: Cut paper, melt butter or dissolve sugar, and you still have paper, butter and sugar. Burn paper or bake a cake, and you get something new.
A physical change changes size, shape or state, but it is still the same substance. A chemical change makes a new substance.

head: Physical changes
Chemical changes
rows: Burning wood or a candle wick

blocks.html: Signs of a chemical change: bubbles of a new gas, a new color, light or heat given off, or a new smell. (Bubbles alone are not proof: boiling water bubbles too.)

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Burning: light, heat, ash
Baking: a new texture and smell
Rusting: a new reddish color
Fizzing: a new gas

blocks.cap: Signs that something new has formed.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: An apple slice turns brown after an hour on the counter. Physical or chemical?
steps: The brown color is new.
It formed because the apple reacted with oxygen in the air.

blocks.html: Calling melting a chemical change. Melted ice is still water and can freeze again. A burnt piece of toast cannot be turned back into bread.
In any change, the total mass stays the same if nothing escapes. When baking soda fizzes in vinegar in an open cup, the cup gets lighter because the gas floats away.

items: Do this in a sink or on a tray, with a grown-up.
Put a spoonful of baking soda in a cup and add a little vinegar.
What signs of a chemical change do you see? (The bubbles are a new gas, carbon dioxide.)

blocks.html: Going further. Try mixing safely on screen in the Mixing Lab. Michael Faraday's The Chemical History of a Candle is a classic for older readers.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-PS1-4: whether mixing two or more substances results in new substances

blocks.html: Kick a ball, pull a wagon, open a door: each time you use a force.
A force is a push or a pull. A force can start something moving, stop it, make it faster or slower, or change its direction.

Forces have a size (strong or weak) and a direction. When two equal forces push opposite ways, as in a tug-of-war that nobody is winning, they are balanced and nothing changes. When one side is stronger, the forces are unbalanced and the rope moves toward it.

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Kick: a push starts it
Sled: a pull
Magnet: a pull without touching
Falling apple: gravity pulls

blocks.cap: Some forces need touching; magnets and gravity work from a distance.

blocks.title: Balanced or unbalanced?
blocks.q: Two children push a box from opposite sides. One pushes hard, one pushes gently. What happens?
steps: The pushes are not equal, so the forces are unbalanced.
The box moves the way the harder push points.
blocks.a: The box slides away from the child pushing hard.

blocks.html: Thinking a moving thing needs a push to keep going. A puck on smooth ice glides a long way. Things slow down because friction or air pushes against them.

items: Roll a toy car across a smooth floor. Then give it a gentle push from the side while it rolls.
What changed: its speed, its direction, or both?

blocks.html: Going further. Newton's Laws of Motion in the Science Lab, and Forces in Physical Science when you are older.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-PS2-1: balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object

blocks.html: Slide a book across a carpet and across a smooth table. On the carpet it stops quickly. A force is pushing against it: friction.

Friction is a force between two surfaces that rub together. It acts against the motion. Rough surfaces make more friction, smooth ones less. Gravity is a pull between things; Earth's gravity pulls everything toward the center of the Earth.
Friction is often helpful. It lets your shoes grip, your bike brakes stop and a match light. Sand on an icy path adds friction. Oil and wheels make friction smaller.
Every surface has tiny bumps, even ones that feel smooth. When two surfaces slide, the bumps catch on each other.
"Down" is toward the center of the Earth everywhere, which is why people in Australia do not fall off. Gravity also holds the Moon near the Earth.

blocks.title: Which falls first?
blocks.q: You drop a heavy book and a light book flat from the same height at the same time. Which lands first?
steps: Gravity makes both fall faster and faster at the same rate.
Air pushes on both, but these are both heavy and flat-shaped enough that it hardly matters.
blocks.a: They land at almost the same time.

blocks.html: Thinking heavy things always fall much faster. A feather falls slowly because air pushes it, not because it is light. On the Moon, which has no air, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather in 1971, and they landed together.

items: Make a ramp with a board or a big book. Let a toy car roll down onto a bare floor, then onto a towel.
Measure how far it goes each time. Which surface has more friction?

blocks.html: Going further. In the Book Cart lab, push a cart and change the friction.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-PS2-1: the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down

blocks.html: Long ago, people moved huge stones with logs and poles. A pole that turns on a point is a lever, one of the six simple machines.

blocks.name: sciexp-machines
blocks.cap: The six simple machines: lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane (ramp), wedge and screw.

blocks.html: A lever is a stiff bar that turns on a point called the fulcrum. The push you give is the effort; the thing you lift is the load. The farther your push is from the fulcrum, the less push you need.

blocks.name: sciexp-lever
blocks.cap: Move the push point. A load of 6 blocks, 2 steps from the fulcrum, needs only 3 blocks of push at 4 steps: 6 × 2 = 3 × 4.

blocks.html: A lever balances when load × its distance = effort × its distance. A far-away push needs less force, but your hand moves farther. You trade distance for force.

blocks.title: How much push?
blocks.q: A rock weighing 10 blocks sits 1 step from the fulcrum. You push 5 steps from the fulcrum. How many blocks of push balance it?
steps: Load × distance: 10 × 1 = 10.
Effort × 5 must make 10.

blocks.html: Levers are everywhere: a seesaw, a crowbar, a bottle opener, scissors (two levers), a broom and even your arm, with the elbow as the fulcrum.
Thinking a lever gives free energy. You push less, but your end moves a long way while the load moves a little.

items: Lay a ruler across a pencil to make a seesaw. Put three coins at one end.
Press down on the other end with one finger. Then slide the pencil closer to the coins and press again.
When is it easiest? When the fulcrum is close to the load.

blocks.html: Going further. The Trebuchet Workshop is a giant lever that throws. Archimedes studied levers over 2,000 years ago: see Archimedes: The Works (the young readers' path). Later, Levers in Physical Science.
A doorknob, a steering wheel and a screwdriver handle all look different, but they work the same way: a big wheel turns a small axle.

In a wheel and axle, a big wheel and a small rod (the axle) turn together. Turning the big wheel takes less force to turn the axle. A pulley is a wheel with a rope in its groove. A fixed pulley changes the direction of your pull. A movable pulley halves the pull you need.

blocks.name: sciexp-machines

items: wheel
pulley

blocks.cap: A wheel and axle, and a pulley.

head: Pulley setup
To lift 20 pounds you pull about
Rope you pull for each foot of lift
rows: Two ropes each holding half, plus more pulleys

blocks.html: (Real pulleys have a little friction, so you pull a bit more than this.)

blocks.title: Raising a flag
blocks.q: Why does a flagpole have a pulley at the top?
steps: You cannot climb up to lift the flag.
The fixed pulley lets you pull the rope down at the bottom to raise the flag up.
blocks.a: It changes the direction of the pull.

blocks.html: Thinking a single fixed pulley makes things lighter. It only lets you pull in an easier direction.

items: Hang a broom handle between two chairs. Tie a rope to a bag with a few books in it.
Loop the rope over the broom handle and pull down to lift the bag. You made a simple fixed pulley (with lots of friction).

blocks.html: Movers push heavy boxes up a ramp into a truck instead of lifting them straight up. The ramp is an inclined plane.

An inclined plane (ramp) lets you raise a load with a smaller push, but along a longer path. A wedge is two ramps back to back: it splits or cuts (an ax, a knife, a doorstop). A screw is a ramp wrapped around a post.

blocks.name: sciexp-machines

items: ramp
wedge
screw

blocks.cap: A ramp, a wedge and a screw.

blocks.html: Lifting a box 1 meter straight up takes a big force over a short path. Pushing it up a 4-meter ramp to the same height takes about a quarter of the force (plus a bit for friction), over four times the path.

blocks.title: Long or short ramp?
blocks.q: Ramp A is 2 meters long, ramp B is 6 meters long. Both reach the same truck. Which needs less push?
steps: Both raise the box the same height.
The longer ramp spreads the work over a longer path.
blocks.a: Ramp B, the longer one, needs less push.

blocks.html: Mountain roads zig-zag for the same reason: a longer, gentler path is easier to climb. A jar lid and a corkscrew are screws.
Thinking the longer ramp is harder because it is longer. Each step is easier; there are just more of them.

items: Tie a string to a toy car with a few coins taped on, and hook a rubber band to the string.
Pull it straight up to a stack of books, then up a ramp to the same stack. Watch how far the rubber band stretches each time.
Less stretch means less force.

blocks.html: Going further. Simple Machines in Physical Science explains the numbers. To build a chain of ramps, a wedge and a screw lift yourself, try the Contraption Workshop.
A running dog, a glowing lamp, a ringing bell and a warm stove all have something in common: energy.
Energy is what makes things move, light up, heat up or make sound. It comes in many forms.

head: Form
Examples
rows: a rolling ball, wind, a running child
food, a battery, a stretched rubber band, a book on a high shelf
a stove, a warm mug, the Sun's warmth
a lamp, the Sun, a firefly

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Battery: stored
Bulb: light and heat
Drum: sound
Skater: motion
Bread: stored in food
Sun: light and heat

blocks.cap: Energy in many forms.

blocks.html: The faster something moves, the more motion energy it has. A fast ball hits harder than a slow one.

blocks.title: Find the energy
blocks.q: A child holds a stretched slingshot band, then lets go and the pebble flies. What forms of energy are there?
steps: The stretched band holds stored energy.
When it snaps back, the pebble gets motion energy.
The snap makes a little sound.
blocks.a: Stored energy, then motion (and a little sound).

blocks.html: Thinking only moving things have energy. Food has stored energy that your body uses, and a ball held high has stored energy that turns into motion when it falls.

items: Walk through your home and list ten things that use or give off energy.
Next to each, write the form: motion, stored, heat, light, sound or electrical. Many have more than one!

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-PS3-1: the speed of an object is related to the energy of that object

blocks.html: Switch on a flashlight and it glows. Where does the light come from? From energy stored in the battery.
Energy is never used up. It changes form or moves from one thing to another.

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Stored
Electrical
Light
Heat

blocks.cap: A flashlight: stored → electrical → light (and heat).

blocks.html: When a ball rolls to a stop, its motion energy did not vanish. It turned into a little heat in the floor and the ball (from friction) and a little sound.

blocks.title: Follow the energy
blocks.q: A child eats breakfast, then rides a bike to school. Trace the energy.
steps: The food holds stored energy.
The body changes it into motion of the legs and some heat.
The pedals pass motion to the wheels.

blocks.html: Saying the battery's energy "disappears". It changed into light, heat, sound or motion.

items: Rub your hands together fast for ten seconds. What do you feel?
Your motion energy turned into heat by friction.

blocks.html: Going further. In Pendulums, watch energy swap between height and motion. Later: Conservation of Energy in Physical Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-PS3-4: a device that converts energy from one form to another

blocks.html: Hold a mug of hot cocoa and your hands warm up. Put an ice cube in your hand and your hand gets cold. Heat is on the move.

Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things, never the other way by itself. It moves three ways: by touching (conduction), by moving air or water carrying it (convection), and by rays through space, like sunshine (radiation).

blocks.name: sciexp-measure
blocks.cap: A room at 22 °C (about 72 °F).

head: Conductors (heat moves through fast)
Insulators (heat moves through slowly)
rows: Air trapped in a foam cup or a coat

blocks.html: A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot all the way up because metal passes heat along quickly. A wooden spoon stays cool at the top because wood is an insulator.

blocks.title: The sweater test
blocks.q: Does a sweater make you warm by making heat?
steps: A sweater has no energy source.
It traps air, an insulator, so your own body heat escapes slowly.
blocks.a: No: it keeps your body heat in.

blocks.html: Thinking cold "moves in". Your hand feels cold on ice because heat leaves your hand and goes into the ice.

items: Wrap one ice cube in a sock or a mitten and leave another bare on a plate.
Check every 15 minutes. Which melts first? The insulator slows heat from reaching the ice.

blocks.html: Going further. The Laws of Thermodynamics in the Science Lab, and Heat Transfer in Physical Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-PS3-2: energy can be transferred from place to place by heat

blocks.html: A fridge magnet holds up a drawing. A compass needle points north. Both are magnets.
Every magnet has a north pole (N) and a south pole (S). Opposite poles attract (N and S pull together). Like poles repel (N and N, or S and S, push apart).

blocks.name: sciexp-magnets
blocks.cap: Flip a magnet to see the poles attract or repel.

blocks.html: Magnets pull on things made of iron or steel (and a few other metals, like nickel). They do not pull on wood, plastic, paper, glass, aluminum, copper or gold. The pull works through paper and even through your hand.

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Steel paper clip
Copper penny
Steel bolt
Plastic spoon
Iron key
Aluminum foil

blocks.cap: Sort the things: does a magnet pull them?

blocks.title: Push or pull?
blocks.q: The north pole of one magnet faces the north pole of another. What happens?
steps: Both facing poles are N: like poles.
Like poles repel.

blocks.html: Thinking magnets attract all metals. Foil, pennies and soda cans (aluminum) do not stick.
The Earth itself is a giant magnet. A compass needle is a small magnet that turns to line up with it, so its north end points north.

items: Take a fridge magnet on a hunt around the kitchen. Test spoons, foil, cans, coins and the fridge door.
Make two lists: sticks and does not stick. Were any metals on the "does not" list?

blocks.html: Going further. William Gilbert showed in 1600 that the Earth is a magnet: Gilbert: On the Loadstone. Later: Magnets in Physical Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-PS2-3: electric or magnetic interactions between two objects not in contact

blocks.html: A flashlight has a battery, a bulb, a switch and metal strips joining them. Together they make a circuit.

Electricity flows only around a complete loop, a closed circuit: out of one end of the battery, through the wires and the bulb, and back into the other end. If the loop has a gap, it is an open circuit and the bulb stays dark.

blocks.name: sciexp-circuit
blocks.cap: Tap the switch to open and close the circuit.

blocks.html: A switch is a little bridge in the loop. Turned on, it closes the gap. Turned off, it opens the gap and the current stops.
The battery pushes electric charges around the loop like a pump pushing water around a ring of pipes. A break anywhere stops the whole flow.

blocks.title: Will it light?
blocks.q: A wire goes from the top of a battery to a bulb, but no wire goes from the bulb back to the battery. Does the bulb light?
steps: The current needs a path out and a path back.
There is no path back, so the loop is open.

blocks.html: Thinking one wire is enough because "the electricity goes to the bulb". It must go through the bulb and back.

items: With a grown-up, open a flashlight and take out the batteries.
Look for the metal spring and strips that touch each end of the batteries, the switch and the bulb. Trace the loop with your finger.
Never take apart anything that plugs into the wall, and never put anything into an outlet.

blocks.html: Going further. Build circuits safely on screen in the Circuit Builder. Later: Circuits in Physical Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-PS3-2: energy can be transferred from place to place by electric currents

blocks.html: Look at a lamp cord: a soft plastic coat outside, shiny copper wire inside. Why both?
Conductors let electricity flow through them easily: metals like copper, aluminum, iron and silver. Insulators stop it: plastic, rubber, wood, glass, cloth and paper.

blocks.name: sciexp-circuit
blocks.cap: A circuit with a gap. Here a strip of foil bridges the gap. Foil is a metal, a conductor, so the bulb lights.

blocks.name: sciexp-circuit
blocks.cap: Now a rubber eraser bridges the gap. Rubber is an insulator, so the bulb stays dark.

blocks.html: The copper inside a wire carries the current. The plastic outside keeps the current in the wire and keeps people safe.

blocks.title: Test the coin
blocks.q: A steel coin is put across the gap in a circuit. Does the bulb light?
steps: Steel is a metal.
Metals are conductors.

blocks.html: Thinking anything shiny conducts. Shiny plastic or a shiny painted pencil does not. Metal does, even when it is dull or rusty-looking.
Water from a tap carries electricity well enough to be dangerous, which is why we keep electrical things away from sinks and baths.

items: Collect a spoon, a key, a pencil, a plastic cup, a rubber band, a piece of foil and a paper clip.
Guess which are conductors. Then build each one into the gap in the Circuit Builder, or check against the table above.

blocks.html: In 1820 a Danish professor, Hans Christian Ørsted, noticed during a lecture that a compass needle jumped when he switched on a current in a nearby wire. Electricity can make magnetism!
A coil of wire with electricity flowing through it is a magnet, an electromagnet. Wrap it around an iron nail and it gets stronger. Switch off the current and it stops being a magnet.

blocks.name: sciexp-circuit
blocks.cap: An electromagnet: a battery, a switch and a coil of wire around an iron nail. Close the switch and the nail picks up paper clips.

head: Make it stronger
Why
rows: each turn adds to the magnet
the iron becomes a magnet too

blocks.html: Electromagnets are in doorbells, speakers, cranes that lift scrap cars, and electric motors. A motor uses electromagnets pushing and pulling on magnets to make something spin: a fan, a mixer, a toy car.

blocks.title: Why use one?
blocks.q: A scrapyard crane lifts a car, moves it and drops it in a pile. Why use an electromagnet instead of a regular magnet?
steps: A regular magnet cannot be switched off.
An electromagnet lets go the moment the current stops.
blocks.a: So it can drop the car when the current is switched off.

blocks.html: Thinking an electromagnet stays magnetic forever. It is a magnet only while the current flows (a steel nail may keep a little magnetism).

items: Hold a compass near a running electric fan or hair dryer (do not open them). Does the needle move?
Look for motors around the house: anything that spins when you switch it on.

blocks.html: Going further. Michael Faraday turned this idea into the first motor and generator: Faraday: Experimental Researches in Electricity. Later: Electromagnets in Physical Science.
Stand in the sun and a dark shape follows you: your shadow. Why is it there?
Light travels in straight lines. When something blocks it, the place behind it gets no light: a shadow. The closer the object is to the light, the bigger its shadow.

blocks.name: sciexp-shadow
blocks.cap: Slide the block toward the lamp and away. Watch the shadow on the wall grow and shrink.

blocks.html: Things that block light make shadows: we call them opaque, like wood or your hand. Transparent things, like clear glass, let light through. Translucent things, like wax paper, let some through.
Rays from the lamp spread out in straight lines. Close to the lamp, the block stops a wide fan of rays, so a big patch of wall goes dark.

blocks.title: Puppet show
blocks.q: You want a giant shadow puppet on the wall. Where do you hold your hand?
steps: Shadows grow as the object gets closer to the light.
blocks.a: Close to the flashlight, far from the wall.

blocks.html: Thinking a shadow is a kind of reflection or is made of something. It is only the place the light cannot reach.

items: In a dark room, shine a flashlight on a wall. Make hand shadows.
Move your hand toward the light and away. Measure the shadow's width with a ruler each time.
Outdoors, never look straight at the Sun.

blocks.html: Going further. The Optics Bench shows light rays.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-PS4-2: light reflecting from objects and entering the eye allows objects to be seen

blocks.html: How do you see this page? Light from a lamp or a window hits the page, bounces off, and goes into your eyes.

We see things when light bounces off them into our eyes. A smooth mirror reflects light neatly: it leaves at the same angle it came in. Light also bends (refracts) when it passes from air into water or glass.

blocks.name: sciexp-light
blocks.cap: A ray hits a mirror and bounces off at the same angle.

blocks.name: sciexp-light
blocks.cap: A straw in a glass of water looks broken where it enters the water, because light from the straw bends at the water's surface.

blocks.html: Light slows down a little in water and glass. Like a cart rolling from pavement into sand at a slant, it turns as it slows. Lenses in glasses and magnifying glasses use this bending.

blocks.title: Periscope
blocks.q: A periscope has two mirrors. How does it let a submarine crew see above the water?
steps: Light from above hits the top mirror and bounces down the tube.
The bottom mirror bounces it sideways into the viewer's eye.
blocks.a: The two mirrors pass the light down and into the eye.

blocks.html: Thinking light comes out of our eyes. In a dark room with no light at all, you see nothing: there is no light to bounce off things.

items: Put a pencil in a clear glass half full of water. Look from the side. Does it look broken?
Put a coin in an empty cup and move your head back until the rim just hides it. Hold still while someone slowly pours in water. The coin appears!

blocks.html: Going further. The Optics Bench, and Refraction in Physical Science.
In 1666 young Isaac Newton made a hole in his window shutter and let a beam of sunlight through a glass prism. On the wall appeared a band of colors.

White light is a mix of all the colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet (the letters ROY G BIV help you remember). A prism, or raindrops, bend each color a different amount and spread them apart.

blocks.name: sciexp-light
blocks.cap: A prism spreads white light into a spectrum. Violet bends the most, red the least.

blocks.html: A rainbow appears when the Sun is behind you and rain is in front of you. Each raindrop acts like a tiny prism.

A red apple looks red because it reflects red light and soaks up the other colors. A white shirt reflects all colors; a black one soaks up nearly all of them, which is why black clothes get hot in the sun.

blocks.title: Under red light
blocks.q: In a room lit only by red light, what color does a white sheet of paper look?
steps: White paper reflects whatever light hits it.
Only red light hits it.

blocks.html: Thinking the prism adds the colors. Newton showed the colors were in the sunlight already; a second prism can mix them back into white.

items: On a sunny morning, stand with your back to the Sun and spray a fine mist from a garden hose.
Look for a rainbow in the spray. Which color is on the outside of the bow?
Or set a glass of water on a sunny windowsill and look for colors on the floor.

blocks.html: Going further. Newton: Optics (the young readers' path tells this story), and Color in Physical Science.
Put your fingers gently on your throat and hum. You can feel a buzz. That buzz is a vibration, and it makes sound.

Sound is made when something vibrates (moves back and forth quickly). The vibration passes through the air (or water, or a solid) to your ears. Fast vibrations make a high pitch; slow ones make a low pitch. Bigger vibrations are louder.

blocks.name: sciexp-sound
blocks.cap: Change the pitch and the loudness. High pitch: waves close together. Loud: tall waves.

head: Change
What you hear
rows: Shorter or tighter string, smaller drum
Longer or looser string, bigger drum

blocks.html: Sound needs something to travel through. In space there is no air, so there is no sound: astronauts talk by radio. Sound travels faster through water and solids than through air. Put your ear on a table while someone taps the far end!

blocks.title: Which is higher?
blocks.q: A big tuba and a small flute play. Which usually plays higher notes?
steps: Small instruments have short tubes and fast vibrations.

blocks.html: Mixing up loud and high. A lion's roar is loud and low; a mouse squeak is soft and high.

items: Stretch rubber bands of different thickness around an open box or a plastic tub.
Pluck each. Which sounds higher: thin or thick? Tight or loose?
Fill glasses with different amounts of water and tap them gently with a spoon. Which is highest?

blocks.html: Going further. Learn to read the notes in Music; see waves in Pendulums and Resonance; and later Sound in Physical Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-PS4-1: a model of waves

blocks.html: The water in your glass may once have been part of a cloud, a glacier or the ocean. Earth's water goes round and round in the water cycle.

blocks.name: sciexp-cycle
blocks.cap: The water cycle. The Sun powers it.

blocks.html: Evaporation: the Sun warms water and it rises as invisible water vapor. Condensation: high up, the vapor cools into tiny drops that make clouds. Precipitation: drops join, grow heavy and fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail. Collection: water gathers in oceans, lakes, rivers and under the ground, and the cycle starts again.
Plants add water vapor to the air too, from tiny holes in their leaves. Most of Earth's water, about 97 out of every 100 drops, is salty ocean water.
When seawater evaporates, the salt stays behind. That is why rain is fresh water even though so much of it came from the salty ocean.

blocks.title: Name the step
blocks.q: On a cold morning, drops of water form on the outside of a glass of ice water. Which step is that?
steps: The drops came from water vapor in the air.
The cold glass cooled the vapor into liquid drops.

blocks.html: Thinking clouds are made of water vapor or smoke. Clouds are made of tiny drops of liquid water or bits of ice, so small they float.

items: Put a little warm water in a clear bowl and cover it with plastic wrap. Set a few ice cubes on top of the wrap.
Watch for a few minutes. Drops form under the wrap (condensation) and drip back down (precipitation).

blocks.html: Going further. The Water Cycle in Earth Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-ESS2-2: amounts and percentages of salt water and fresh water

blocks.html: Is it hot or cold? Windy or still? Sunny, cloudy, rainy or snowy? That is the weather: what the air is like at a place right now.
Weather is measured with tools: a thermometer (temperature), a rain gauge (how much rain fell), a wind vane (which way the wind blows from), an anemometer (wind speed) and a barometer (air pressure).

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Thermometer: temperature
Rain gauge: rainfall
Wind vane: wind direction
Anemometer: wind speed

blocks.cap: Weather tools.

blocks.name: sciexp-measure
blocks.cap: A cool spring day: 15 °C, about 59 °F.

blocks.html: Climate is different from weather. Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years: a desert has a dry climate even if it rains one day.

head: Clouds
What they often mean
rows: fair now; a change may be coming

blocks.title: Weather or climate?
blocks.q: "It snowed in our town last Tuesday." Weather or climate?
steps: It tells about one day.

blocks.html: A wind vane points to where the wind comes from. A "north wind" blows from the north toward the south.

items: Keep a weather journal for two weeks: the temperature, the clouds, the wind and any rain or snow each day.
Make a rain gauge: a straight-sided jar outside, away from trees. Measure the water with a ruler after it rains, then empty it.

blocks.html: Going further. Weather and Climate in Earth Science, and the Weather and Climate course for teens.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-ESS2-1: represent data to describe typical weather conditions
Next Generation Science Standards, 3-ESS2-2: climates in different regions

blocks.html: Pick up a pebble. It may have been a mountain, the floor of a sea or melted rock deep underground.
Minerals are natural solids with their own pattern of particles, like quartz, mica or salt. Rocks are made of one or more minerals. There are three kinds of rock, named for how they form.

head: Kind
How it forms
Examples
rows: melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens
layers of sand, mud, shells or pebbles are pressed and cemented together
heat and pressure deep underground change a rock without melting it

blocks.name: sciexp-cycle
blocks.cap: The rock cycle: any kind of rock can become any other, over a very long time.

blocks.html: Fossils are found mostly in sedimentary rock, because plants and animals were buried in the soft layers before they hardened.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: A rock has layers like a stack of pancakes and a fossil shell in it. Which kind is it most likely?
steps: Layers and fossils come from sediments settling and being pressed.

blocks.html: Thinking rocks never change. Rocks change all the time, only slowly: the rock cycle can take millions of years.

items: Collect a few rocks from a yard, a park or a path (where collecting is allowed).
Look at each with a hand lens. Do you see crystals, grains of sand or layers?
Scratch each with a steel nail. Quartz is harder than steel and will not scratch; chalk and many softer rocks will.

blocks.html: Going further. Agnes Giberne's The World's Foundations is a classic geology book for young readers. Later: The Rock Cycle in Earth Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-ESS1-1: patterns in rock formations and fossils

blocks.html: The Grand Canyon is more than a mile deep. A river did most of the digging, a grain at a time, over millions of years.
Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces. Erosion carries the pieces away. Deposition drops them somewhere else, where they build new land.

head: What does it
How
rows: rivers and waves grind rock; rain wears it
water in cracks freezes, expands and splits rock
roots grow into cracks and pry them open
pulls rocks and soil downhill in landslides

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: A river carves a valley
Ice splits rock
Wind carries sand
Roots crack rock

blocks.cap: Things that weather and erode the land.

blocks.html: Rivers drop their sand and mud where they slow down, often where they meet the sea. That builds a delta, like the Nile Delta or the Mississippi Delta.

blocks.title: Which is it?
blocks.q: Rain washes soil off a bare hillside into a stream. Weathering or erosion?
steps: The soil was already in small pieces.
It is being carried away.

blocks.html: Thinking weathering and erosion are the same. Weathering breaks; erosion moves.

items: Outdoors or in a tray, build a small hill of sand or soil.
Pour water slowly from a cup at the top. Watch where it carries the sand and where it drops it.
Do it again with a few stones and leaves pressed into the hill. Do they slow the erosion?

blocks.html: Going further. Weathering and Erosion and Deposition in Earth Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-ESS2-1: the effects of weathering or the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind or vegetation

blocks.html: You eat to get food. A tree never eats a thing, yet it grows huge. Where does its food come from?

Plants make their own food in their leaves. They use sunlight for energy, water from their roots and carbon dioxide, a gas in the air. They make a sugar for food and give off oxygen. This is called photosynthesis.

blocks.name: sciexp-plant
blocks.cap: Sunlight, water and carbon dioxide go in; sugar is made and oxygen comes out.

head: Part
Job
rows: hold the plant and take in water and minerals
holds the plant up and carries water and food
make food from sunlight, water and air

blocks.html: Most of a tree's wood is built from carbon dioxide taken out of the air and water from the ground. The soil gives only a few minerals. Scientists weighed soil before and after growing a tree in it and found the soil had lost almost nothing.

blocks.title: In the dark
blocks.q: A plant is kept in a dark closet for two weeks with water. What happens?
steps: Without light, it cannot make food.
blocks.a: It turns pale and weak, and it may die.

blocks.html: Thinking plants get their food from the soil. Soil gives water and minerals, but the food is made in the leaves.

items: Put a water plant from a fish store, or a leaf, into a clear glass of water in bright sunlight.
After an hour or two, look for tiny bubbles on the leaves. That gas is oxygen the leaf gave off.

blocks.html: Going further. Plants Make Food (Young Learners) for younger brothers and sisters, and Photosynthesis in Life Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-LS1-1: plants get the materials they need for growth chiefly from air and water

blocks.html: A rabbit eats grass. A fox eats the rabbit. The energy in the fox's dinner came, in the end, from the Sun.

Producers (plants and algae) make food from sunlight. Consumers eat other living things: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both. Decomposers (mushrooms, bacteria, worms help too) break down dead plants and animals and return their minerals to the soil.

blocks.name: sciexp-chain

items: sun
grass
rabbit
fox

blocks.cap: A food chain. Each arrow points from the food to the eater.

blocks.html: Most animals eat more than one thing, and are eaten by more than one thing. When we draw all the chains together, they make a food web.

blocks.name: sciexp-chain
blocks.cap: A meadow food web.

blocks.html: If the rabbits all disappeared, the foxes and hawks would have less to eat, and the grass might grow taller. A change in one part of a web changes the others.

blocks.title: Read the arrows
blocks.q: In the chain seeds → mouse → owl, what does the owl eat?
steps: The arrow points from the food to the eater.
The arrow into the owl comes from the mouse.

blocks.html: Reading the arrows backward. "Grass → rabbit" means energy goes from the grass to the rabbit: the rabbit eats the grass.

items: Write down everything you ate yesterday.
For each food, trace it back to a producer. (Cheese → cow → grass. Bread → wheat.) Does every chain start with a plant?

blocks.html: Going further. Run a whole ecosystem in Predators and Prey, and see Food Webs in Life Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-LS2-1: the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment

blocks.html: A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat. A camel can go days without drinking. Each is built for the place it lives.
An adaptation is a body part or a behavior that helps a living thing survive and have young where it lives.

blocks.name: sciexp-pic

items: Webbed feet
Spines and a waxy stem
Big eyes for night
A hump of fat

blocks.cap: Adaptations help each living thing fit its home.

blocks.html: Some adaptations are behaviors: bears hibernate, birds migrate, possums play dead. Camouflage (colors that hide) and mimicry (looking like something dangerous) are adaptations too.

blocks.title: Which fits?
blocks.q: An animal has a long sticky tongue and strong claws for digging. What might it eat?
steps: Claws dig into nests; a sticky tongue picks up tiny things.
blocks.a: Ants or termites (it is an anteater).

blocks.html: Thinking an animal grows an adaptation because it wants or needs it. A giraffe does not stretch its neck longer by trying. Adaptations are passed down from parents to young over many, many generations.

items: Watch birds at a feeder or in a park. Look at their beaks: short and thick, long and thin, hooked?
Guess what each eats. (Thick beaks crack seeds; thin ones probe for insects and nectar.)

blocks.html: Going further. Structural Adaptations in Life Science, and the young readers' path of Darwin: The Origin of Species.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-LS1-1: internal and external structures that support survival, growth, behavior and reproduction

blocks.html: Your body is made of systems, teams of parts that work together. They all have to work at once, even while you sleep.

blocks.name: sciexp-body
blocks.cap: Some of the body's organs.

head: System
Main parts
Job
rows: hold you up and protect organs
move the bones and pump the heart
carry oxygen and food all around the body
take in oxygen, breathe out carbon dioxide
break food into pieces the body can use

blocks.html: Body systems work together. When you run, your muscles need more oxygen, so you breathe faster (respiratory) and your heart beats faster (circulatory), all controlled by your brain (nervous).
Muscles can only pull, not push. That is why they work in pairs: one muscle bends your elbow, another straightens it.

blocks.title: Which system?
blocks.q: Which system carries the oxygen from your lungs to your toes?
steps: Blood carries oxygen.
The heart pumps the blood through blood vessels.

blocks.html: Thinking the heart sits far over on the left. It is near the middle of the chest, tipped a little to the left, and about the size of your fist.

items: Find your pulse: press two fingers gently on the inside of your wrist below your thumb.
Count the beats in 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Now jump in place for one minute and count again. What changed, and why?

blocks.html: Going further. William Harvey discovered how blood goes around the body: Harvey: On the Motion of the Heart and Blood. Later: Body Systems Working Together in Life Science.
Every morning the Sun appears in the east, crosses the sky and sets in the west. It looks as if the Sun moves around us. It is really the Earth that turns.

The Earth spins (rotates) on its axis once about every 24 hours. The half facing the Sun has day; the half facing away has night. Because Earth spins toward the east, the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west.

blocks.name: sciexp-sky
blocks.cap: Turn the Earth. The dot is you: is it day or night where you are?

blocks.html: Shadows change during the day too. In the morning and evening, when the Sun is low, shadows are long. Near noon, when the Sun is high, they are short. A shadow always points away from the Sun.

blocks.name: sciexp-shadow
blocks.cap: A stick's shadow during the day.

blocks.title: Count the turns
blocks.q: How many times does the Earth spin in one week?
steps: It spins once a day.
A week has 7 days.

blocks.html: Thinking the Sun goes around the Earth, or that night comes when the Moon covers the Sun. Night is our side of Earth turned away from the Sun.

items: In a dark room, shine a lamp (the Sun) at a ball or an orange (the Earth). Stick a small sticker on it for your town.
Turn the ball slowly. When is your sticker in day? In night? At sunrise?
Outdoors, push a stick into the ground and mark the end of its shadow at breakfast, lunch and dinner. Never look straight at the Sun.

blocks.html: Going further. Agnes Giberne's Sun, Moon, and Stars, the Sky and Solar System lab, and Day and Night in Earth Science.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-ESS1-2: patterns of the length and direction of shadows, day and night

blocks.html: Some nights the Moon is a round, bright ball. Some nights it is a thin smile. Some nights you cannot see it at all. The Moon has not changed shape; we see different amounts of its lit half.

The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight. One half of it is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon travels around the Earth, about once every 29½ days, we see more or less of that lit half. These are the phases.

blocks.name: sciexp-sky
blocks.cap: The phases of the Moon, in order: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

head: Phase
About how many days after new moon
What you see
rows: the right half lit (seen from the Northern Hemisphere)

blocks.html: Waxing means growing (more lit each night); waning means shrinking. Gibbous means more than half lit.

blocks.title: A week later
blocks.q: Tonight is a full moon. What phase will it be in about one week?
steps: After full, the Moon wanes.
About a week after full comes the last quarter.

blocks.html: Thinking the Earth's shadow makes the phases. The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which happens only now and then, about twice a year.

items: Draw the Moon every clear night for a month, and write the date.
Or: in a dark room, use a lamp as the Sun and hold a ball at arm's length as the Moon. Turn slowly in a circle and watch the lit part of the ball change.

blocks.html: Going further. Sky and Solar System, and Moon Phases in Earth Science.
Our solar system is the Sun and everything that goes around it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets like Pluto, asteroids and comets.

The Sun is a star, a huge ball of hot, glowing gas. The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Gravity keeps them going around the Sun.

blocks.name: sciexp-sky
blocks.cap: The Sun and its planets in order (sizes and distances are not to scale).

head: Planet
One fact
rows: closest to the Sun; a year is only 88 days
the hottest planet, with thick clouds
the only planet known to have life
the red planet, with a giant volcano
the biggest planet, with a Great Red Spot
bright, wide rings of ice and rock

blocks.html: The first four are small and rocky. The outer four are giants made mostly of gas or ice. A sentence can help you remember the order: "My Very Eager Mother Just Served Us Noodles."
The Sun looks bigger and brighter than other stars only because it is much closer. Its light takes about 8 minutes to reach us; light from the next nearest star takes over 4 years.

blocks.title: Which planet?
blocks.q: Which planet is fourth from the Sun?
steps: Mercury 1, Venus 2, Earth 3, Mars 4.

blocks.html: Thinking the Sun is not a star. It is an ordinary star, the closest one to us.

items: On a long hallway or sidewalk, make a model with steps: Sun at 0, Mercury 1 step, Venus 2, Earth 2½, Mars 4, Jupiter 13, Saturn 24, Uranus 48, Neptune 75.
How far apart are the outer planets compared with the inner ones?

blocks.html: Going further. Fly a spacecraft in the Orbit Lab; see The Solar System in Earth Science; read Sun, Moon, and Stars, and the young readers' path of Copernicus: On the Revolutions.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-ESS1-1: the apparent brightness of the Sun compared with other stars is due to their distances from Earth
